It would be easy to treat the coincidence itself as damning, as though the instinct must be corrupted simply because it happens to match what's administratively convenient.

Would this same caution, this same PT-first plan, have been reached in a world where nobody was counting opioid numbers this quarter? If the answer is yes, the plan is sound and its origin doesn't taint it. If the answer is uncertain, that uncertainty itself is the thing to notice before the note gets written, not after.
Ordering imaging in that case wouldn't be extra caution — it would be defensive documentation dressed up as thoroughness, and that's its own kind of dishonesty, just aimed at a different audience.
Naming the trap and stopping would be a kind of abdication — it hands the clinician a worry without giving them anything to do with it.

The point isn't to talk the clinician out of their instinct or into it — it's to give them the tools to find out which one it actually is, on this patient, today, and to write that down in a form specific enough to mean something later.
